rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second ṣirāṭ is a fully matching apposition to the first; Ibn Mālik calls it the corresponding or matching apposition to avoid applying ‘whole’ to God in 14:1–2.
rows.anchor: صِرَاطَ الذين أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ } بدل من الصراط الأول بدل الكل من الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apposition reinforces the predication, since it repeats the governing relation, and explains the straight path as the Muslims’ path, emphatically attesting to its rightness.
rows.anchor: وفائدة الإبدال تأكيد النسبة بناءً على أن البدل في حكم تكرير العامل والإشعار بأن الصراط المستقيم بيانه وتفسيره صراط المسلمين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative analysis calls the second phrase an adjective of the first ṣirāṭ.
rows.anchor: وقيل صفة له

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One unusual transmitted interpretation treats the second path as different from the first, as if a conjunction were understood.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب المنقول أن الصراط الثاني غير الأول وكأنه نوى فيه حرف العطف

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad identifies the path with knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
rows.anchor: فعن جعفر بن محمد هو العلم بالله والفهم عنه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is conformity between inward and outward life in the full bestowal of blessing.
rows.anchor: وقيل موافقة الباطن للظاهر في إسباغ النعمة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation makes the path adherence to obligations and Prophetic practices; al-Ālūsī dismisses it as a departure from the straight path.
rows.anchor: وقيل التزام الفرائض والسنن ، ولا يخفى أن هذا القول خروج عن الصراط المستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim; this is also transmitted from ʿUmar and the Ahl al-Bayt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود وزيد بن علي صراط من أنعمت عليهم ، وهو المروي عن عمر وأهل البيت رضي الله تعالى عنهم

rows.speaker: الشهاب
rows.claim: Al-Shihāb takes the indefinite relative expression man as evidence that an indefinite name may be applied to God; al-Ālūsī calls this an evident confusion because the genitive is objective, not agentive.
rows.anchor: قال الشهاب : وفيه دليل على جواز إطلاق الأسماء المبهمة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines bestowal as conveying beneficence to another rational being, so one does not say that someone bestowed a favor on his horse.
rows.anchor: والإنعام إيصال الإحسان إلى الغير من العقلاء كما قاله الراغب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported definition calls a blessing a benefit given by someone superior to a person without compensation.
rows.anchor: قيل : إن النعمة نفع الإنسان من دونه لغير عوض

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view identifies those blessed as believers in general.
rows.anchor: واختلف في هؤلاء المنعم عليهم فقيل المؤمنون مطلقاً

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view restricts those blessed to the prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل الأنبياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view means the followers of Moses and Jesus before textual alteration and abrogation.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصحاب موسى وعيسى عليهما السلام قبل التحريف والنسخ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies those blessed as the Companions of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view names Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar as those blessed.
rows.anchor: وقيل محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبو بكر وعمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers Ibn ʿAbbās’s report in al-Ṭabarī: the blessed include prophets, angels, martyrs, the truthful, and all who obey and worship God; other views restrict the class to some members.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن المراد بالذين أنعمت عليهم الأنبياء والملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unrestricted blessing embraces every blessing, in line with the verse saying that people cannot enumerate God’s blessings.
rows.anchor: ولم يقيد الأنعام ليعم { وَإِن تَعُدُّواْ نِعْمَةَ الله لاَ تُحْصُوهَا }

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says God blessed them by creating them for felicity.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنعم عليهم بخلقهم للسعادة . وقيل بأن نجاهم من الهلكة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says God blessed them by rescuing them from destruction; a further view says the blessing was guidance.
rows.anchor: وقيل بأن نجاهم من الهلكة . وقيل بالهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using the active second-person verb is an appeal: since God has already bestowed favor, the worshipper asks Him to grant guidance too; the cited verse of poetry illustrates that God taught people to ask in order to give.
rows.anchor: وفي بناء أنعمت للفاعل استعطاف فكأن الداعي يقول أطلب منك الهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accompanying poem says that God would not have taught people to ask unless He intended to grant their hopes; al-Ālūsī gives no poet’s name.
rows.anchor: لو لم ترد نيل ما نرجو ونطلبه *** من فيض جودك ما علمتنا الطلبا

rows.speaker: اللغويون
rows.claim: The linguists list ten forms: hāʾ ḍamma/kasra with variable mīm and optional wāw or yāʾ. Attributions name Ḥamza, the majority, al-Ḥasan, ʿUmar b. Khālid/Fāʾid, Ibn Kathīr/Qālūn, al-Aʿraj, Muslim b. Jundub, Ibn Hurmuz, and al-Khaffāf from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وحكى اللغويون في { عَلَيْهِمْ } عشر لغات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr is a matching apposition to alladhīna. Making it an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim is semantically awkward; the relative clause still contains its pronoun because the antecedent is not truly discarded.
rows.anchor: { غَيْرِ المغضوب عَلَيْهِمْ وَلاَ الضالين } بدل من { الذين } بدل كل من كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating ghayr as an adjective meaning different is weak: ghayr has become a noun and usually does not modify an expressed noun.
rows.anchor: والبدل بالوصف ضعيف ضعيف لأنها غلبت عليها الاسمية

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh analyzes ghayr as an explanatory or restrictive adjective of alladhīna; al-Ālūsī explains that the relative is definite generically but can function like an indefinite when only an unspecified subset is intended.
rows.anchor: وعن سيبويه أنها صفة { الذين } مبينة أو مقيدة

rows.speaker: المحققون من علماء العربية
rows.claim: Some authoritative Arab grammarians allow ghayr to become definite by annexation between two opposite definite terms, as in movement versus stillness; this analysis is adopted by those who rely on it.
rows.anchor: لأن المحققين من علماء العربية قالوا إنها قد تتعرف بالإضافة وذلك إذا وقعت بين متضادين معرفتين

rows.speaker: ابن السري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrī says ghayr becomes definite when annexed to a definite having only one opposite, since the contrast is then exclusive.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن السري وغيره : إذا أضيفت { غير } إلى معرف له ضد واحد فقط تعرفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection from 35:37 does not disprove this definiteness: ṣāliḥan may be a fronted circumstantial accusative, or ghayr alladhī may be an apposition to it.
rows.anchor: لجواز أن يكون { صالحا } حالاً قدمت على صاحبها

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; a noncanonical report attributes the same reading to Ibn Kathīr. It is best parsed as a circumstantial accusative governed by anʿamta, though other analyses are discussed.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى عنه { غَيْرِ } بالنصب ، وروي ذلك شاذاً عن ابن كثير

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash permits the accusative as either a disconnected or connected exception if bestowal is understood generally.
rows.anchor: وجوز الأخفش أن يكون النصب على الاستثناء المنقطع أو المتصل إن فسر الإنعام بما يعم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ rejects the exception analysis because ghayr then means siwā and the negative lā cannot be coordinated with it unless lā is treated as extra; al-Ālūsī notes the usage after wāw is unattested.
rows.anchor: ومنعه الفراء لأنه حينئذٍ بمعنى سوى فلا يجوز أن يعطف عليه ( بلا ) لأنها نفي

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: A report ascribed to al-Akhfash treats the exception as semantically negative, allowing lā to coordinate by meaning and removing al-Farrāʾ’s objection.
rows.anchor: وحكى بعضهم عن الأخفش أن الاستثناء في معنى النفي ، فيجوز العطف عليه ( بلا )

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl parses the accusative as governed by an omitted verb, aʿnī, and al-Ālūsī endorses him: exception is problematic and the circumstantial analysis requires an unpersuasive indefinite ghayr.
rows.anchor: وعند الخليل النصب بفعل محذوف أعني : أعني وبه أقول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some posit an ellipsis, supplying ghayra ṣirāṭ al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim, and offer several possible syntactic attachments; al-Ālūsī prefers the unelliptical straightforward syntax.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : في الآية حذف والتقدير غير صراط المغضوب عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of anger denotes intensity; the word is also used for a hard rock, a vicious snake, and a scowling she-camel.
rows.anchor: والغضب أصله الشدة ، ومنه الغضبة الصخرة الصلبة الشديدة

rows.speaker: السعد
rows.claim: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge.
rows.anchor: فسر تارة بحركة للنفس مبدؤها إرادة الانتقام كما في «شرح المفتاح » للسعد

rows.speaker: السعد
rows.claim: In his commentary on al-Kashshāf, al-Saʿd defines divine anger as the will to take revenge.
rows.anchor: كما في «شرح المفتاح » للسعد وتارة بإرادة الانتقام كما في «شرح الكشاف » له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A definition in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid describes anger as a state of the soul followed by the spirit’s outward motion seeking revenge; another account calls it a change when the heart’s blood boils.
rows.anchor: كما في «شرح المقاصد » .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith warns people to beware of anger, likening it to a glowing ember in the heart and pointing to swollen neck veins and reddened eyes; no grading or source is given here.
rows.anchor: اتقوا الغضب فإنه جمرة تتوقد في قلب ابن آدم ألم تروا إلى انتفاخ أوداجه وحمرة عينيه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority.
rows.anchor: وفي «الكشاف » معنى غضب الله تعالى إرادة الانتقام من العصاة وإنزال العقوبة بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the early generations, al-Ālūsī affirms anger as an eternal divine attribute fitting God’s majesty without specifying how or claiming to know its reality, like mercy.
rows.anchor: وأنا أقول كما قال سلف الأمة : هو صفة لله تعالى لائقة بجلال ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith God’s mercy preceded His anger means either that mercy’s effects are greater or that mercy appeared earlier.
rows.anchor: محمول على الزيادة في الآثار أو تقدم ظهورها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in the verses about being lost in the earth and God destroying deeds; in religion it means departing from truth.
rows.anchor: وأصل الضلال الهلاك ومنه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب السختياني
rows.claim: Abū Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads al-ḍāʾallīn with hamza, avoiding two adjacent quiescent letters although their meeting is permissible.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو أيوب السختياني { وَلاَ الضألين } بإبدال الألف همزة

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd records the dialectal forms daʾaba and shaʾaba; this pronunciation is also found in ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd’s reading of 55:39.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو زيد دأبة وشأبة وعلى هذه اللغة قراءة عمرو بن عبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poem’s word fādaʾhamat exemplifies the same hamzated form; grammarians disagree whether the usage can be extended by analogy.
rows.anchor: فادهأمت وهل يقاس عليه أم لا ؟ قولان

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A reading with wa-ghayr in place of wa-lā is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr; the muṣḥaf’s mutawātir reading is wa-lā, which reinforces the negation implicit in ghayr.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى عنه وعبد الله بن الزبير أنهما كانا يقرآن

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Aḥmad transmits and Ibn Ḥibbān grades as ḥasan a Prophetic report identifying the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians.
rows.anchor: وحسنه ابن حبان في «صحيحه » مرفوعاً إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits the same identification from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd; Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he knows no disagreement among Qurʾān commentators about it.
rows.anchor: وأخرجه ابن جرير عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī also reads the general terms broadly: those erring in outward works, such as sinners, are under anger; those erring in belief are astray. The Prophetic Jewish and Christian identifications remain sound specifications of the general wording.
rows.anchor: بل الأولى أن يحمل المغضوب عليهم على كل من أخطأ في الأعمال الظاهرة وهم الفساق

rows.speaker: من زعم
rows.claim: Some argue Jews and Christians are too mild a referent because atheists and polytheists are worse; al-Ālūsī rejects this reasoning in light of the sound Prophetic report and criticizes its disregard of hadith.
rows.anchor: فمن زعم أن الحمل على ذلك ضعيف لأن منكري الصانع والمشركين أخبث ديناً من اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report.
rows.anchor: والعجب من الإمام الرازي أنه نقل هذا ولم يتعقبه بشيء سوى أنه زاد في الشطرنج بغلاً

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some support the Jewish identification from the verse saying that God cursed and became angry with a group, making some of them apes and swine.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعضهم على أن المغضوب عليهم هم اليهود بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some support the Christian identification from the verse warning against following the desires of a people who went astray.
rows.anchor: وعلى أن الضالين النصارى بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the hadith as evidence: anger and straying are also ascribed generally to unbelievers, and both terms apply specifically to Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: والأولى الاستدلال بالحديث لأن الغضب والضلال وردا جميعاً في القرآن لجميع الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He offers several reasons for the order: Jews precede Christians historically; bestowal contrasts with retribution rather than misguidance; and Jews are more obstinate, corrupt, hostile to believers, and abased.
rows.anchor: وإنما قدم سبحانه المغضوب عليهم على الضالين مع أن الضلال في بادئ النظر

rows.speaker: السلفي والديلمي وابن عدي
rows.claim: Al-Salafī, al-Daylamī, and Ibn ʿAdī transmit a report saying that whoever has no charity should curse the Jews; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وورد في الحديث : «من لم يكن عنده صدقة فليلعن اليهود » رواه السلفي والديلمي وابن عدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says Christians are less culpable and closer to Islam, and a person who is merely astray may still find guidance.
rows.anchor: والنصارى دون ذلك وأقرب للإسلام منهم ولذا وصفوا بالضلال لأن الضال قد يهتدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews rejected both Jesus and Muḥammad, while Christians rejected only Muḥammad; al-Ālūsī also says Jewish scandals and atrocities exceed those of Christians.
rows.anchor: أنهم كفروا بنبيين محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وعيسى عليه السلام والنصارى كفروا بنبي واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that the Christian doctrine of Trinity is no worse than Jewish claims that God is poor, His hand is tied, and Ezra is His son.
rows.anchor: وقول النصارى/ بالتثليث ليس أفظع من قول اليهود

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the delayed mention of the astray by the rhyme of the verse endings; al-Ālūsī accepts this only alongside the other explanations.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : تأخير الضالين لموافقة رؤوس الآي ولا بأس بضمه إلى تلك الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness.
rows.anchor: وإنما أسند النعمة إليه تعالى تقرباً والمقصود طلب الهداية إلى صراط من ثبت إنعام الله تعالى عليه

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athīr and al-Tanūkhī classify passivizing a verb after addressing its agent as an unusual kind of rhetorical turn; al-Ālūsī accepts it if turn means stylistic variation, and also defends the technical reading through al-Sakkākī’s definition.
rows.anchor: وقد عد ابن الأثير في «كنز البلاغة » والتنوخي في «الأقصى القريب » بناء الفعل للمفعول بعد خطاب فاعله

rows.speaker: جبريل
rows.claim: Abū Maysara reports that Gabriel taught the Opening to the Prophet and instructed him to say Āmīn after wa-lā al-ḍāllīn; the report is cited from Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Bayhaqī without a grading.
rows.anchor: عن أبي ميسرة : «أن جبريل أقرأ النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī reports the Prophet’s instruction that the congregation say Āmīn when the imam recites the final words, so that God will love them; Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, and Ibn Abī Shayba transmit it.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الحنفية
rows.claim: The Ḥanafīs conceal Āmīn, following ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; the Shāfiʿīs say it aloud. The report of the majority’s loud recitation is interpreted as instruction or discussion.
rows.anchor: وإخفاؤها مذهب ساداتنا الحنفية ، وهو مذهب أمير المؤمنين علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the imam should not say Āmīn because he is the supplicant; this is also found in a less famous report from Abū Ḥanīfa, whereas the famous view is that he says it silently.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن لا يقولها الإمام لأنه الداعي

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
rows.claim: Reports from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal and Anas, cited from al-Kashshāf, say the Prophet concealed Āmīn.
rows.anchor: وروى الإخفاء عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عبد الله بن مغفل وأنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āmīn is not part of the Qurʾān by consensus; a slight pause separates it from the sūra. Al-Ālūsī rejects Mujāhid’s contrary attribution as utterly false because it appears in no muṣḥaf.
rows.anchor: وليست من القرآن إجماعاً ولذا سن الفصل بينها وبين السورة بسكتة لطيفة

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: Some authorities say that anyone who claims Āmīn is Qurʾān has committed unbelief.
rows.anchor: حتى ذكر غير واحد أن من قال : إن آمين من القرآن كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āmīn is an Arabic particle functioning as a verb, built on fatḥa to avoid meeting two quiescent letters; its correct meaning is respond, while another view gives it a broader sense including a synonym.
rows.anchor: وهي اسم فعل مبني على الفتح كأين لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says Āmīn is used for a broader meaning that includes respond and its synonym.
rows.anchor: وقيل موضوعة لما هو أعم منه ومن مرادفه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A strange view derives the Arabicized word from the foreign hamīn because fāʿīl is not an Arabic pattern; a response says it may be a unique pattern with analogues, or originally short and lengthened.
rows.anchor: ومن الغريب ما قيل إنه عجمي معرب همين لما أن فاعيل كقابيل ليس من أوزان العرب ورد بأنه يكون وزناً لا نظير له وله نظائر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another unusual view treats Āmīn as a name of God because it contains a hidden pronoun referring to Him; al-Ālūsī finds this rationale even stranger.
rows.anchor: ومن العجيب ما قيل إنه اسم الله تعالى والقول في توجيهه أنه لما كان مشتملاً على الضمير المستتر الراجع إليه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers disagree whether the alif in Āmīn is inherently long or short; groups support each origin.
rows.anchor: وقد تمد ألفه وتقصر وإلى أصالة كل ذهب طائفة

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī calls a doubled mīm a dialect form; another view calls it an error. Since Āmīn is a non-Qurʾānic supplication with a sound meaning, some say that pronunciation does not invalidate prayer.
rows.anchor: وأما تشديد ميمه فذكر الواحدي أنه لغة فيه

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports a sound-chain hadith in which the Prophet tells Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that no Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qurʾān passage equals the Opening, calling it the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qurʾān granted to him.
rows.anchor: ما روي بأسانيد صحيحة عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه : «أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم خرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls the sūra the Mother of the Book and a treasure of gnosis; he says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events, Muslim rulers’ names, their histories, and their fates from it, likening it to the Preserved Tablet of what appears in existence.
rows.anchor: فهي أم الكتاب والحاوية من دقائق الأسرار العجب العجاب حتى إن بعض الربانيين استخرج منها الحوادث الكونية وأسماء الملوك الإسلامية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī closes by praying for the sūra’s lights to shine upon him and for access to its hidden secrets, declaring God the source of success and guide to verified truth.
rows.anchor: نسأل الله تعالى أن يمن علينا بإشراق أنوارها والاطلاع على مخزونات أسرارها إنه ولي التوفيق
